variants.name: Interface-based passive view (classic)
variants.idiom_name: IView interface + presenter class; form/control implements it, test double substitutes
variants.implementation_notes: The classic .NET shape: declare an IView (properties for queries, methods for display, events for gestures), implement it in the Form/Window/UserControl, and give the presenter the IView plus the model. The view's widget events call presenter methods; the presenter updates the view only through the interface, so MSTest/xUnit can run it against a hand-written stub with no message loop. Use this form whenever the screen has real logic; for purely mechanical field mapping prefer the binding-based variant below.
pitfalls: Event subscriptions hold strong references: unsubscribe in Dispose/Detach or a closed form stays reachable through the model's or the presenter's event list.
An async presenter callback resumes on a thread-pool thread; touching WinForms/WPF controls off the UI thread throws or corrupts state - marshal via Control.Invoke or SynchronizationContext.
Default interface members (C# 8+) are inherited behaviour in the contract, but properties with backing fields are not allowed, so view state must still live in the concrete view.

variants.name: Data-binding Supervising Controller
variants.idiom_name: INotifyPropertyChanged model/view-model + BindingSource/simple binding; presenter handles input and complex logic
variants.implementation_notes: Fowler's Supervising Controller flavor in .NET: the screen's simple fields are mapped by the binding engine - controls bind through a BindingSource to an object (often the model or a small view-model) that raises PropertyChanged - and the presenter (controller) only handles user gestures and the effects binding cannot express, such as enabling a cancel button or colouring a variance value. This removes most manual Show/Sett calls but reintroduces untested view behaviour, so it pays off when the screen is mostly field mapping. Use the interface-based variant when all view updates must stay testable.
pitfalls: Forgetting PropertyChanged (or raising it with a wrong property name) silently freezes the bound control; use CallerMemberName and bind by name consistently.
Binding to a view-model and also mutating the control directly creates two sources of truth and update loops; pick one direction per field.
Simple binding keeps the control alive through the BindingSource; clear DataBindings/DataSource when the screen is disposed.
